rationale: Initial characterization of dominant RNU2-2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy by Chiu et al. observed hippocampal sclerosis on brain MRI in 3 of 5 patients (60%) and sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges in 4 of 5 patients (80%), with mesial temporal sclerosis also noted in individual drug-resistant cases (Lilles et al.). Furthermore, hippocampal sclerosis is not a typical hallmark of RNU4-2 ReNU syndrome. However, the claim that this specific dual combination is present in >50% of dominant RNU2-2 individuals broadly fails to replicate or generalize across larger multi-center cohorts: major systematic studies of dominant RNU2-2 variants (Greene et al., n=25; Leit�ao et al., n=35) describe severe early-onset epilepsy, microcephaly, hypotonia, and hyperventilation, but do not find or report structural hippocampal sclerosis in a majority (>50%) of patients.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 5 patients with dominant RNU2-2 DEE, 3 individuals displayed hippocampal sclerosis on brain MRI and 4 individuals had sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges on EEG.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 25 individuals with recurrent dominant de novo mutations in RNU2-2 (positions 4 and 35), the phenotype is characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, hypotonia, severe complex epilepsy, and episodic hyperventilation, without hippocampal sclerosis reported as a majority neuroimaging feature.

source.title: Mutations in the small nuclear RNA gene RNU2-2 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent epilepsy
source.quote: The disorder is characterized by intellectual disability, autistic behavior, microcephaly, hypotonia, epilepsy and hyperventilation. All cases display a severe and complex seizure phenotype.

evidence.text: A nationwide cohort analysis identified 35 individuals with recurrent dominant pathogenic variants in RNU2-2 presenting with developmental delay, severe intellectual disability, and frequent epilepsy, but hippocampal sclerosis was not identified as a defining >50% feature distinguishing it from other spliceosomal NDDs.

source.title: Systematic analysis of snRNA genes reveals frequent RNU2-2 variants in dominant and recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
source.quote: We report RNU2-2 variants in 141 individuals, including 35 with recurrent dominant pathogenic variants and 91 affected members from 73 families with biallelic variants.

conflicts: Small initial case series (Chiu et al., n=5) reported hippocampal sclerosis in 3/5 (60%) and sleep-activated multifocal discharges in 4/5 (80%), whereas larger multi-center dominant cohorts (Greene et al., n=25; Leit�ao et al., n=35) highlight severe refractory seizures, hyperventilation, hypotonia, and microcephaly without establishing hippocampal sclerosis in >50% of dominant individuals.

It remains unproven whether hippocampal sclerosis is an intrinsic primary neurodevelopmental feature of dominant RNU2-2 or an acquired secondary sequela of prolonged status epilepticus and recurrent febrile/hemiclonic seizures occurring in early childhood.

new_directions.question_text: Is hippocampal sclerosis in dominant RNU2-2 DEE an acquired pathology secondary to early status epilepticus rather than a primary malformation?
new_directions.rationale: High frequencies of status epilepticus (5/5 in Chiu et al.) may trigger secondary excitotoxic hippocampal sclerosis, meaning its absence in patients imaged early does not preclude the diagnosis.

new_directions.question_text: What is the true prevalence of sleep-potentiated epileptiform activity across a standardized multi-center cohort of RNU2-2 patients undergoing nocturnal video-EEG monitoring?
new_directions.rationale: Overnight sleep EEG is required to systematically test whether sleep activation of multifocal spikes is a universal or majority hallmark compared to routine awake EEG recordings.
